C0.quote: We consider the notions of agreement, diversity, and polarization in ordinal elections
C0.note: Borderline. The main object is indices of election profiles rather than a decision procedure. Their computation rests on k-Kemeny, a Kemeny-type aggregation (compared to Chamberlin-Courant), so ELIG was chosen as the first-listed code.

C1.quote: There is a polynomial-time 5.4-approximation algorithm for k-Kemeny.
C1.note: OT: the paper proposes new diversity and polarization indices. SI: indices are evaluated on synthetic datasets, some resampled from real data. AL and SI are about equally central; AL was chosen as the first listed.

C2.1.value: election; preferences (or, votes); preference order (his or her vote)
C2.1.quote: voters whose preferences (or, votes ) are represented as linear orders

C2.2.quote: are represented as linear orders over C

C2.3.quote: each voter has a preference order (his or her vote)
C2.3.note: Preferences and views are attributed to voters but are identified with the vote.

C2.4.quote: voters whose preferences (or, votes ) are represented as linear orders
C2.4.note: Preferences and votes are used interchangeably. There is occasional 'report' language, but no statement or reason about submission.

C3.2.note: Preferences are equated with votes by terminology only; there is no statement that voters submit them.

C4.1.note: No utility, welfare, satisfaction or cost notions are used for voters.

C5.1.note: Indices measure agreement, diversity and polarization, not welfare or representation.

VOT.quote_behav: under impartial culture (IC) each vote is drawn uniformly at random
VOT.note: Votes are exogenous, generated from statistical cultures.

C8.1.note: NA: no type is STRAT or MIXED.

C9.1.note: Claims concern whether the indices capture diversity and polarization, not institutions, voter well-being or rule choice.
